body: Bollards in Czechia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back. This design is only shared with Slovakia.
Czechia and Slovakia both use a special wide Type B guardrail, which is unique in Europe. Czechia uses this type more consistently than Slovakia.
Czechia and Slovakia commonly use wide, round concrete poles, which are often attached in pairs.
Czech and Slovak poletops typically feature short metal bars holding the insulators.
Poletops with two support bars creating an upside-down triangle can be found in Czechia and Slovakia, but also in Germany, Albania, Serbia, and Romania.
Less common but unique to Czechia and Slovakia are concrete poles with trident poletops, which have two arms angled upwards.
Both Czechia and Slovakia have lamp posts with a thick base mounted by opposing pairs of bolts.
Temporary square signposts with red and white stripes are common in both Czechia and Slovakia.
Czech and Slovak chevrons are typically white with red arrows, or less commonly, red on yellow.
Striped utility poles for gas and water can be found in Czechia and Slovakia, but similar poles exist elsewhere in Europe, so caution is needed.

Czechia and Slovakia are known for their unique hiking markers, which consist of a colorful stripe between two white ones, sometimes forming an arrow. Similar markers can be found in Poland, Hungary, and Germany.
Well-maintained and often vibrantly colored panel apartment buildings are a feature of Czechia and Slovakia, distinguishing them from other former Eastern Bloc countries.
Roofs with diamond-shaped tiles are common in Czechia and Slovakia, and to a lesser extent, Hungary.
A grey tape on the car antenna is a common meta for Generation 3 coverage in Czechia and Slovakia, but it's also seen in Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria.
In Generation 4 coverage, look for black signs at the end of bridges, which display the road number on the left.
To distinguish between Czech and Slovak, look for unique letters. Czech has Ř, Ě, and Ů, while Slovak has Ĺ, Ô, Ä, Ŕ, and Ĺ. Both languages use acute accents on vowels.
The Czech landscape consists of rolling hills. In contrast, Slovakia has both taller mountains and more completely flat areas.
Czechia often has solid outer road lines with no center line, a feature also common in Germany.
Czechia uses arrow-shaped directional signs with a filled-in tip, which are recognizable from behind. Slovakia uses small white arrows instead.
Czech road signs have a border that is separated from the edge by a colored strip. In Slovakia, the border is usually right on the edge.
Czech highway signs have a double border: a thin white border separated from the edge by a second colored border. Slovak highway signs have a single white border on the edge.
Czechia commonly uses bright red or blue street signs. The Czech word for street is 'ulice', differing from the more common 'ulica' in other Slavic languages.
Czech house numbers are typically on blue or red signs with thin white borders. Slovak house numbers are usually on white signs.
Czech signposts often have thick, black caps, a feature not typically seen in Slovakia.
Czech pedestrian signs have five stripes. The stripes on Slovak signs are on a smaller scale.
Czech road signs use a relatively thin font, while Slovak signs use a bolder font. The Czech font is similar to that used in Luxembourg and Germany.
Czech kilometre markers have a yellow outline and no black horizontal middle line. Slovak markers have a black horizontal middle line and no yellow outline.
Bicycle signs in Czechia are yellow. You may also see hiking-style markers with yellow stripes instead of white.
Suburban houses in Czechia are often connected in pairs, which is less common in neighboring countries.
Much of the Generation 3 coverage in Czechia was filmed during winter, resulting in grey or snowy landscapes, which is uncommon in Slovakia.
Czech railway crossing signs have no background, whereas Slovak ones have a white rectangular background.
Unlike Slovakia, Czechia has a small amount of Generation 2 coverage.
Czech road numbers generally follow a geographical pattern. Roads starting with 1-5 are mostly regional, while 7, 8, and 9 start in Prague and go north.
Four-digit bike paths follow a clockwise numbering pattern starting in Southern Bohemia. Paths starting with 'A' are unique to Prague.
Czech phone numbers have 9 digits with a 1-3 digit area code. Unlike Slovak numbers, they do not typically begin with a 0.
The Moravian wine region produces about 95% of all Czech wine.
The landscape of northern Bohemia is characterized by rolling hills combined with steep, solitary hills, which sometimes have castles on top.
Timber-framed houses in Czechia are mostly found along the northern border with Germany.
Houses with thick, dark wooden poles supporting the upper floors are common in the northernmost parts of Czechia.
Dark wooden houses with white stripes visible between the wood are common in northern Czechia.
Townhouses in Moravia are often long, connected in groups, and have abnormally large front doors resembling barn doors. This style is also common in northeastern Austria.
Selské Baroko (folk baroque) architecture, characterized by highly decorated walls in small villages, is found around České Budějovice.
Houses with single-pane windows are more common in the northwestern parts of Czechia.
Blue street signs are more common in the east of Czechia, with Ostrava being a major city that uses them.
A white street sign with blue text and a red border is typical of Slovakia, so finding one in Czechia suggests you are near the Slovak border.
White street signs with red text are most common in eastern and southern Czechia, and are notably used in Brno.
White street signs with blue text are most common in the eastern and central-northern parts of Czechia.
White street signs with black text are most common in the southeastern part of Czechia.
